terms.comment: The medieval word for an assembly, from Old French parlement; Milton’s for the Parliament of the English Commonwealth, and Traupman’s for a parliament today. A member of parliament is parlāmentārius (Traupman 356) or populī lēgātus (Levi–Bini p. 21); a chamber of parliament, camera (M-O).

terms.gloss: the assemblies of the Roman people
terms.comment: Rome had no parliament. The people voted laws in these assemblies, on a magistrate’s proposal, and elected the magistrates there, while the senate only advised (see senate). A parliament is an elected assembly of representatives that makes the laws itself.
Milton and Tursellinus call the English Parliament and the Paris parlement senātus (Morgan–Owens).

terms.gloss: the elected deputies; the lower house
terms.grammar: noun phrase, plural: lēgātus with the adjective populāris
terms.comment: Levi and Bini’s phrase for a chamber of deputies; for a senate whose members sit for life they keep senātus.

phrases.english: the Parliament of the Commonwealth of England
phrases.source: Milton (1674), in M-O s.v. legislature, parliament
